papers.title: Spiritual self-care practice and mindfulness among patients with cancer: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the correlation between spiritual self-care practices and mindfulness among cancer patients in southeast Iran. METHODS: This descriptive, correlational, cross-sectional study was conducted on a convenience sample of 600 eligible cancer patients. Data were collected using three instruments: a demographic and clinical characteristics questionnaire, the Spiritual Self-Care Practice Scale, and the Relaxation, Meditation, and Mindfulness Trait Tracker (RMMtm 3.1). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26, employing both descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including multivariate regression analysis. RESULTS: The mean total score for spiritual self-care practice among cancer patients was 3.17 ± 1.15, which was above the questionnaire's midpoint. Mindful emotion had the highest mean score (3.78 ± 1.67), followed by mindful focus (3.20 ± 1.57) and mindful relaxation (3.14 ± 1.65). Multivariate regression analysis revealed that 63.9% of the variance in spiritual self-care was explained by variables including mindful emotion ( SIGNIFICANCE OF THE RESULTS: The study findings indicate a significant relationship between spiritual self-care practice and dimensions of mindfulness. Nurses can address patients' spiritual self-care practice needs by implementing the nursing process and empowering them through interventions that enhance mindfulness.

papers.title: "It Does Tend to Be a Sort of One-Size-Fits-All Approach": Perceptions and Experiences of Staff Teaching Neurodivergent Students in Veterinary Clinical Learning Environments.
papers.abstract: Clinical learning environments (CLEs) are integral in veterinary education, providing short placements of hands-on learning in clinical practices at veterinary schools or external practices. Staff must facilitate neurodivergent (ND) students' reasonable adjustments, while balancing teaching and other competing interests, while university-designed support plans are based on the traditional academic environment. CLEs are usually commercial businesses where students are taught by academic and non-academic clinical staff, the latter often having limited educational training. Understanding CLE staff's attitudes, perceptions, and experiences is required to enable optimal student support. A questionnaire investigated these attributes at one UK veterinary school. Thirty-two staff responded; 12 undertook follow-up interviews. Mixed-method data analysis was performed. Most participants agreed ND students need extra support in CLEs; opinion differed about how and to what extent. Some participants expected ND students to become "more resilient" as they considered reasonable adjustments would not be available following graduation. Additional individual student information, including strategies and accommodations on other placements, was wanted. Staff attitudes to neurodiversity awareness training varied widely. Training barriers included insufficient time, staff workloads, negative attitudes, perceived challenges in implementing training, and lack of relevant training. Conversely, enabling factors included sufficient time, compulsory training, improving training accessibility and flexibility, opportunities to hear from ND individuals, highlighting benefits of training and improved support, and external training. Improving psychological safety in CLEs was identified as critical. Most participants advocated increasing awareness and visibility of neurodiversity, enhancing the clarity of support structures, and providing time to undertake meaningful, relevant neurodiversity training pertaining to CLEs.

papers.title: Effects of brief mindfulness and loving-kindness meditation on associative memory for sad events: A registered report.
papers.abstract: Negative emotion can enhance memory for emotional items while impairing the associative binding and coherence of episodic events. We tested whether a brief combined mindfulness and loving-kindness meditation induction could attenuate sadness-related memory costs for multielement social events. Following preregistration, 113 young adults completed a 20-min mindfulness/loving-kindness meditation induction or matched active control, and 106 were retained for analysis after preregistered exclusions. Participants encoded events composed of a sad or neutral face, an object, and a scene, then completed a four-alternative forced-choice associative memory test and emotional ratings for faces and events. Sad events were remembered less accurately and less coherently than neutral events. However, the mindfulness/loving-kindness meditation induction did not reliably attenuate these memory costs. Bayesian analyses favored the null for associative memory accuracy and remained inconclusive for memory coherence. The intervention also did not reliably modulate emotional responses to sad versus neutral material. Emotional ratings revealed a dissociation between stimulus levels: Sad faces showed the aversive profile, whereas ratings of events were more mixed, suggesting that contextualized social sadness may carry a more complex meaning than a simple aversive cue. These findings identify boundary conditions for brief contemplative inductions and suggest that memory coherence may be an informative end point for future work on emotional memory integration. papers.title: Feasibility of using Making Mindfulness Matter© for children with epilepsy and their parents: A pilot randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Children with epilepsy (CWE) often experience poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), and family environment plays a central role in how CWE cope with challenges. Our aim was to evaluate the feasibility of delivering a family-based mindfulness program (Making Mindfulness Matter©, M3©) synchronously online for CWE and their parents, to support families facing HRQOL-related challenges. METHODS: This was a parallel, 1:1 randomized controlled trial comparing M3© to waitlist control, recruiting families of CWE aged 4-10 years in Ontario, Canada. M3© is an eight-week concurrent parent-child program teaching mindfulness skills for managing stress and building family resiliency, delivered live-online by epilepsy agency staff. Feasibility data were collected through self-administered questionnaires from parents, program facilitators, and research staff. A mixed-methods process evaluation (descriptive statistics, qualitative content analysis) examined participation rate, session attendance, attrition, missing data, quality of session delivery by facilitators, proportion of curriculum units delivered, and participant adherence and satisfaction. RESULTS: Of 298 dyads screened, 72 were randomized (intervention = 35, control = 37; 31 % participation). Time commitment was a key barrier to recruitment and retention. Fifteen M3© groups were completed, and 61 dyads participated. Session fidelity was high (80-100 % curriculum delivered), and most families attended > 75 % of sessions. Families were engaged, practiced skills weekly, and were satisfied with the program. CONCLUSION: M3© was delivered as intended and well-received by participating families, providing preliminary evidence supporting its feasibility as a community-based on-line treatment complementary to clinical care. Findings support further evaluation of M3© in multi-centre trials and highlight time commitment as an important consideration for future recruitment and retention strategies.

papers.title: Impacts of digital third-wave interventions for adults on wellbeing and mental health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: To synthesise the efficacy of digital third-wave process-based interventions (e.g., ACT, Mindfulness, Compassion) for improving wellbeing and ameliorating mental health symptoms in adults. A prospectively registered systematic review (OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/5RMU2) and random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted across six databases through January 2026. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Interventions (k = 147; N = 26,391) yielded small-to-moderate immediate post-intervention improvements in wellbeing (k = 46, g = 0.36), depression (k = 110, g = 0.44), anxiety (k = 93, g = 0.40), stress (k = 66, g = 0.46), quality of life (k = 32, g = 0.30), and psychological flexibility (k = 51, g = 0.41). Heterogeneity was substantial across most outcomes (I2 > 75%). Benefits were observed across healthy (61 trials; n = 15,770), mental health (41 trials; n = 6,130), and medical samples (46 trials; n = 4,491), with population type not significantly moderating immediate post-intervention effects. Comparator type significantly moderated several analyses, with smaller effects against active than inactive controls. Guidance did not significantly moderate immediate post-intervention effects, although it predicted larger short-term depression effects (QM = 4.17, p = .048). At short-term follow-up, effects remained statistically supported across all outcomes, while only depression, anxiety, and stress remained statistically supported at medium-term follow-up. GRADE certainty was moderate for most immediate post-intervention outcomes and low for quality of life. Digital third-wave interventions produced small-to-moderate average benefits across symptom-focused, wellbeing-focused, and process outcomes. Effects were smaller against active comparators, indicating that pooled benefits should be interpreted in relation to comparator intensity. Future research should prioritise rigorous active controls, longer follow-up, and direct tests of whether changes in psychological flexibility mediate improvements in symptoms and wellbeing.
